faq.q: What is Brutalist architecture?
faq.a: Brutalism is a style of concrete or brick left bare and unpainted, and its idea of truthful materials is a principle as well as an appearance. Many link the name to béton brut, the term Le Corbusier used for rough concrete. The Swedish architect Hans Asplund invented the term nybrutalism to describe a brick house designed in 1950; Alison Smithson put "new brutalism" into print in 1953, and Reyner Banham, a critic, took it up in a 1955 essay.

faq.q: What are the key features of Brutalism?
faq.a: Its main mark is concrete or brick left exposed and unpainted. Many brutalist buildings also put their structure and circulation on show. In Sheffield, Park Hill runs broad deck "streets in the sky" along its blocks; Balfron Tower in London places its lifts in a separate tower, joined to the flats by bridges on every third floor; and Boston City Hall's inverted ziggurat makes the work of city government visible on its exterior.

faq.q: Which brutalist buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: Begin with Marseille's Unité d'Habitation (1952) by Le Corbusier, which many cite as the first spark for the style: duplex flats stacked into a vertical neighbourhood along internal streets. Then set it beside Park Hill in Sheffield (1961), Habitat 67 in Montréal (1967) with its stacked prefabricated modules, Denys Lasdun's Royal National Theatre in London (1976) and the Barbican Estate (1982), a walkway city of homes, an arts centre and a lake raised above street level.

faq.q: Where can I see brutalist buildings?
faq.a: The style spread to regions around the world, so there is brutalism on every continent. London has the Barbican, Trellick Tower and the Royal National Theatre; Boston has its City Hall; Le Corbusier's Capitol Complex stands in Chandigarh, India. Further afield are the Kenyatta International Convention Centre in Nairobi, the Bank of London and South America in Buenos Aires and the Museum of Modern Art in Rio de Janeiro.

faq.q: What is modernist architecture?
faq.a: Modernist architecture turns away from ornament and depends on new building technology, leaving volume, structure and plan to do all the design work. It appeared at the close of the 19th century, then was the leading approach from the Second World War to the 1980s, travelling worldwide as the International Style. In the 1920s, Le Corbusier's white houses carried no decoration on either their interiors or their exteriors.

faq.q: What are the principles of modernist architecture?
faq.a: Hitchcock and Johnson's 1932 exhibition at MoMA in New York set out three: buildings conceived as volume, a regular facade in place of symmetry, and no applied ornament. Le Corbusier's Villa Savoye (1931) shows them in practice, combining his Five Points of Architecture in one house, as does the Barcelona Pavilion (1929), where freestanding walls beneath a floating roof let space flow.

faq.q: Which modernist buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: In date order, a short list: the Fagus Factory in Alfeld (1911), where the glass wall wraps the corners without a column; Bauhaus Dessau (1926) and its pinwheel plan; the Barcelona Pavilion (1929); Villa Savoye (1931); Fallingwater (1939), cantilevered above a waterfall; and New York's Seagram Building (1958), set back from a plaza, with bronze mullions that show its frame.

faq.q: Which modernist houses should I study?
faq.a: Houses show modernism's ideas most clearly. Compare the Rietveld Schröder House in Utrecht (1924), De Stijl in three dimensions; Villa Tugendhat in Brno (1930), whose glass walls drop away to the garden; Fallingwater (1939); the Eames House in Los Angeles (1949), built from off-the-shelf industrial parts; Philip Johnson's Glass House (1949); and the Farnsworth House (1951), a single glass room lifted above a floodplain.

faq.q: What is contemporary architecture?
faq.a: Contemporary architecture is what has been built in the 21st century, since 2000, with no one style in the lead. Method shapes it more than style does, and it spans the globe: major new work has gone up in China, Russia and India as well as in Europe and the Americas. Two examples are the Oslo Opera House by Snøhetta (2008) and the CCTV Headquarters in Beijing by OMA (2012).

faq.q: What are the features of contemporary architecture?
faq.a: Current structural systems let buildings be taller, lighter and stronger than twentieth-century ones, and projects are designed as 3D computer models. Some architects prefer natural, ecological materials, and sustainable design treats energy efficiency across a building's whole life as a main aim. The Centre Pompidou-Metz by Shigeru Ban, for instance, roofs its galleries with a woven lattice of glued laminated timber.

faq.q: Which contemporary buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: Useful first examples: Toyo Ito's Sendai Mediatheque (2001), where thin floors rest on thirteen lattice tubes; OMA's Seattle Central Library (2004), whose book spiral is a single continuous ramp; Tate Modern in London (2000), a former power station now used as a museum; the Oslo Opera House (2008); and the Elbphilharmonie in Hamburg (2017) by Herzog & de Meuron, which puts a glass crown on top of a brick warehouse.

faq.q: Where can I see contemporary architecture?
faq.a: Almost anywhere, because the field is global. In Asia and the Middle East there are the CCTV Headquarters in Beijing, the Burj Khalifa in Dubai, once the tallest building in the world, and Foster + Partners' Queen Alia International Airport in Amman. In Europe, see Casa da Música in Porto or the Markthal in Rotterdam; in North America, the High Line in New York.

faq.q: What is deconstructivist architecture?
faq.a: Deconstructivism splits a building into pieces that lack evident harmony, continuity or symmetry, a result many describe as controlled chaos. Its name is a play on Russian Constructivism and draws on the thinking of the French philosopher Jacques Derrida. It first caught public attention through the 1982 Parc de la Villette competition in Paris, and an exhibition at MoMA in 1988 gave the movement its definite shape.

faq.q: Who are the main deconstructivist architects?
faq.a: The 1988 MoMA exhibition curated by Mark Wigley and Philip Johnson brought fame to seven: Zaha Hadid, Rem Koolhaas, Frank Gehry, Daniel Libeskind, Peter Eisenman, Bernard Tschumi and Coop Himmelblau. The label sits uneasily on some of them. Gehry turned it down, as he turned down every label, even though his Guggenheim Bilbao (1997) and Walt Disney Concert Hall (2003) often appear as examples of it.

faq.q: Which deconstructivist buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: Set three side by side: the Wexner Center for the Arts (1989) in Columbus by Eisenman, the Vitra Design Museum (1989) by Gehry and Hadid's first completed building, the Vitra Fire Station (1993); the last two stand in Weil am Rhein. Next look at Libeskind's Jewish Museum Berlin (2001), a zigzag plan crossed by voids that can be seen but not entered, and his Imperial War Museum North in Manchester (2002), made of broken, intersecting curved volumes.

faq.q: Where can I see deconstructivist buildings?
faq.a: Germany has a cluster: the Vitra Design Museum and Vitra Fire Station in Weil am Rhein, BMW Welt in Munich, and the Jewish Museum Berlin. Frank Gehry's work is spread widely, from the Guggenheim Bilbao and the Dancing House in Prague to the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles and the Biomuseo in Panama City. In Rotterdam, OMA's Kunsthal threads ramps through a box.

faq.q: What is parametric architecture?
faq.a: Parametric architecture shapes buildings through algorithms: the designer defines input parameters, and the model updates whenever they shift. Under parametricism, each part of a design is variable and responds to the rest. It avoids both rows of identical repeats and piles of unrelated pieces, seeking spatial complexity that remains readable. Patrik Schumacher introduced the word in 2008, presenting it as following on from modernism and postmodernism.

faq.q: How does parametric design work?
faq.a: The architect writes rules rather than drawing each part: an algorithm takes input parameters, and the model updates whenever one changes, so every element can adapt to the others. Grasshopper, a visual programming tool built on Rhino, is one tool for such models. The Canton Tower in Guangzhou (2010) shows the idea: a lattice of inclined steel columns twisted between two rotated ellipses.

faq.q: Who are the main parametric architects?
faq.a: Patrik Schumacher, who gave parametricism its name, worked with Zaha Hadid; her office designed many of the most familiar examples, such as MAXXI in Rome (2010) and the Heydar Aliyev Center (2012) in Baku. Lars Spuybroek, Greg Lynn, Kas Oosterhuis and Jesse Reiser were among its early practitioners. The wall also includes work by UNStudio, J. Mayer H. and Studio Fuksas.

faq.q: What are good examples of parametric architecture?
faq.a: Four strong examples: Zaha Hadid's Heydar Aliyev Center (2012) in Baku, where one unbroken surface runs from the plaza up over the roof; the Mercedes-Benz Museum (2006) in Stuttgart by UNStudio, whose double-helix ramps sit on a trefoil plan; the Metropol Parasol (2011) in Seville by J. Mayer H., huge timber parasols above a market; and Terminal 3 (2013) of Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport by Studio Fuksas, clad in a double honeycomb skin.

faq.q: What is high-tech architecture?
faq.a: High-tech architecture puts the making and working of a building on show: frame, lifts, stairs and ducts stay visible rather than concealed. It appeared in the 1970s as a kind of late modernism, developed first in Britain. Steel, aluminium and glass are its main materials, and it is often used for factories, offices and galleries.

faq.q: What are the key features of high-tech architecture?
faq.a: Its interiors avoid internal load-bearing walls, leaving floors that can be rearranged, and services like stairs and lifts are often moved out to separate towers. London's Lloyd's Building (1986) wraps a 60-metre atrium with plug-in towers holding its lifts, stairs and ducts, and Hong Kong's HSBC Main Building (1986) suspends its floors from suspension trusses, which frees a public plaza underneath.

faq.q: Who are the main high-tech architects?
faq.a: The leading names are Michael and Patty Hopkins, Norman Foster, Richard Rogers, Renzo Piano and Santiago Calatrava. Many early leaders were British. Their key works on the wall include the Hopkins House in London (1976), Piano and Rogers's Centre Pompidou in Paris (1977), Foster's 30 St Mary Axe in London (2004) and Calatrava's Museum of Tomorrow in Rio de Janeiro (2015).

faq.q: Which high-tech buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: Start with the Centre Pompidou in Paris (1977), whose frame and colour-coded services sit on the outside, leaving open floors and a public piazza. Then set beside it the Lloyd's Building (1986), the HSBC Main Building (1986), Renzo Piano's New York Times Building (2007), screened by ceramic rods, and Menara Mesiniaga (1992) in Malaysia by Ken Yeang, a round tower cooled by sky gardens.

faq.q: What is postmodern architecture?
faq.a: Postmodern architecture restores the things modernism stripped away: ornament, colour, wit and references to history. It arose in the 1960s in reaction to the plainness and uniformity of modern buildings. Credit for launching it goes to Robert Venturi and Denise Scott Brown, and Venturi laid out its case in a 1966 book with the line, "I am for messy vitality over obvious unity." By the late 1990s it had broken up into many new tendencies.

faq.q: What are the key features of postmodern architecture?
faq.a: Postmodern buildings quote history through borrowed elements and allusions, and they use unusual materials. In Philadelphia, the Vanna Venturi House (1964) by Robert Venturi divides a gabled front above a broken arch. The Portland Building (1982) by Michael Graves has giant pilasters and a keystone painted onto a cube-shaped block, and New York's AT&T Building (1984), by Philip Johnson and John Burgee, finishes its granite tower in a broken pediment.

faq.q: Which postmodern buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: Among the most famous works is the Piazza d'Italia (1978) in New Orleans by Charles Moore, a public square whose fountain takes the shape of Italy. Add the Vanna Venturi House (1964), the Portland Building (1982), the Neue Staatsgalerie (1984) in Stuttgart by James Stirling, where a public path ramps through a drum courtyard, and the Sainsbury Wing (1991) of London's National Gallery by Venturi, Scott Brown and Associates.

faq.q: Was postmodern architecture only American?
faq.a: No. America is where it is best known, yet Europe and other regions have notable examples too. In Europe there are Ricardo Bofill's Walden 7 near Barcelona (1975), Piet Blom's Cube Houses in Rotterdam (1984), Hans Hollein's Haas House in Vienna (1990) and Aldo Rossi's Bonnefanten Museum in Maastricht (1995). In Asia, Taipei 101 (2004) stacks eight pagoda-like modules, and Kenzo Tange's Tokyo Metropolitan Government Building (1991) splits into twin towers.

faq.q: What is Art Deco architecture?
faq.a: Art Deco architecture combines strong geometric forms with lavish ornament such as setbacks, sunbursts, metalwork and decorated crowns. It began in Paris during the 1910s, shortly before the First World War, building on the geometry of the Vienna Secession and Cubism. The name was taken from the 1925 exhibition in Paris devoted to decorative and industrial arts. An international style, it was at its height through the 1920s and the early 1930s.

faq.q: What are the key features of Art Deco buildings?
faq.a: Look for strong geometry combined with lavish decoration: decorated crowns, sunbursts, metal ornament and stepped setbacks. Reinforced concrete let architects shape forms with more freedom. New York's Chrysler Building (1930) crowns itself with sunburst arches of stainless steel above its setbacks; Radio City Music Hall (1932) forms its auditorium ceiling from nested semicircles; and Chicago's Adler Planetarium (1930) is a twelve-sided block of rainbow granite.

faq.q: Which Art Deco buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: New York's Chrysler (1930) and Empire State (1931) buildings are the style's best-known skyscraper monuments. Earlier, the Théâtre des Champs-Élysées (1913) in Paris, by Auguste Perret, spanned the auditorium with a concrete frame set behind a flat marble facade. Then compare Detroit's Fisher Building (1928) and its barrel-vaulted arcade with the stepped Kavanagh building (1936) in Buenos Aires.

faq.q: Where can I see Art Deco architecture?
faq.a: Miami Beach has more Art Deco buildings concentrated together than anywhere else in the world, and New York has its skyscrapers, from 30 Rockefeller Plaza to 70 Pine Street. Because the style was international, examples reach far beyond: the Parliament House in Helsinki, the Manila Metropolitan Theater with its Philippine plant motifs, the Australian War Memorial in Canberra and the Estadio Centenario in Montevideo, built for the first World Cup.

faq.q: What is Art Nouveau architecture?
faq.a: Art Nouveau architecture draws its lines from nature, using plant and flower curves, whiplash lines and asymmetry to suggest movement. The earliest Art Nouveau houses were built during the 1890s in Brussels, and from Britain, Belgium and France the style travelled throughout Europe. German speakers call it Jugendstil, a name taken from the art journal Jugend. When the First World War began in 1914, it had largely run its course.

faq.q: What materials did Art Nouveau architects use?
faq.a: Its architects worked with materials new in their day: iron, glass, ceramics and, later on, concrete. In the Hôtel Tassel by Victor Horta in Brussels, a defining example, whiplash ornament and exposed iron columns run through a top-lit stair hall. In Vienna, Otto Wagner's Majolikahaus (1899) clads a flat apartment facade in weatherproof flower-printed tiles, and Hector Guimard took the style onto the street with his Paris Métro entrances.

faq.q: Which Art Nouveau buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: Start in Brussels with two works by Victor Horta, the Hôtel Tassel and Horta House (1901), then Josef Hoffmann's Stoclet Palace (1911). In Glasgow, the Glasgow School of Art (1909) by Charles Rennie Mackintosh fits enormous north-light windows for its studios into a stone facade. In Barcelona, Antoni Gaudí's Casa Batlló (1906) and Casa Milà (1912) show the style at its most sculptural, and Helsinki Central Station (1919) by Eliel Saarinen shows its late granite form.

faq.q: Is Gaudí's work Art Nouveau?
faq.a: On this site it is grouped with Art Nouveau, the movement of his time. Gaudí's buildings share its natural forms and movement but push them into structure: the Sagrada Família, begun in 1882, uses branching tree-like columns and hyperboloid vaults, and the Crypt of Colonia Güell (1914) has leaning columns and vaults found with a hanging model. Park Güell (1914) edges a terrace with a serpentine tiled bench.

faq.q: What is critical regionalism in architecture?
faq.a: Critical regionalism is modern architecture grounded in a particular place, taking local topography, climate and light as its starting point instead of a universal style. It seeks a middle path between architecture's global and local languages, and it turns away from postmodernism's whimsy and ornament. Alexander Tzonis and Liane Lefaivre, both theorists, first put the idea forward in 1981; the historian Kenneth Frampton then took it further.

faq.q: What are the key features of regionalist architecture?
faq.a: Regionalist buildings answer their site, not a style, because Frampton stressed topography, climate and light. Siza's Boa Nova Tea House (1963) tucks low tiled roofs between rocks over the sea. Renzo Piano's Jean-Marie Tjibaou Cultural Centre in Nouméa (1998) sets ten curved timber-ribbed cases that recall Kanak huts, their double skins venting the trade winds, and Luis Barragán's house in Mexico City (1948) turns a blank wall to the street and works with colour and light.

faq.q: Which regionalist buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: Bagsværd Church (1976) near Copenhagen, by Jørn Utzon, is one cited example: inside a plain industrial shell, a billowing concrete ceiling catches the daylight. Set it beside the Boa Nova Tea House (1963) and Leça Swimming Pools (1966) by Siza, the Parliament of Sri Lanka (1982) by Geoffrey Bawa, on its island in a lake, and the Indian Institute of Management Bangalore by Balkrishna Doshi (1983), whose corridors run beneath open pergolas.

faq.q: Who are the main regionalist architects?
faq.a: Its leading architects come from many countries: Jørn Utzon in Denmark, Álvaro Siza in Portugal, Luis Barragán in Mexico, Geoffrey Bawa in Sri Lanka, and Balkrishna Doshi and Charles Correa in India, whose Jawahar Kala Kendra in Jaipur (1991) is laid out on a nine-square plan. That spread follows from the way critical regionalism has developed into separate sub-styles across the world.

faq.q: What makes good museum architecture?
faq.a: Good museum architecture keeps a collection safe while opening it to the public, and each building balances those two duties in its own way. Look at how visitors move through it, where its light comes from and what it does for its city. In Fort Worth, Louis Kahn's Kimbell Art Museum (1972) brings light into its galleries through a slot in cycloid vaults; New York's Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum (1959) is a single spiral ramp.

faq.q: Which museums should architecture students study?
faq.a: Begin with New York's Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum (1959), described as a 20th-century architectural landmark. Then set beside it the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin (1968) by Mies van der Rohe, a single glass hall without columns; the Kimbell Art Museum (1972); Carlo Scarpa's Castelvecchio Museum in Verona (1975); Gehry's Guggenheim Bilbao (1997); Libeskind's Jewish Museum Berlin (2001); and SANAA's 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art, Kanazawa (2004).

faq.q: What is the Bilbao effect?
faq.a: The Bilbao effect is the name given to the pull that Frank Gehry's Guggenheim Bilbao, opened in 1997, had on its city. Cities have long treated museums as engines of economic growth, and this museum's titanium curves were designed with CATIA, an aerospace program. For students, it is a case study of what a museum does for its city, not only for its collection.

faq.q: What are good examples of museums in old buildings?
faq.a: Good examples include Tate Modern in London (2000), a former power station whose Turbine Hall now works as an indoor street, and the Castelvecchio Museum in Verona (1975), Carlo Scarpa's reworking of a medieval castle. Some museums take over buildings whose first use has ended; others attach new wings to old buildings, as the Louvre Pyramid (1989) by I. M. Pei in Paris does, lighting an underground hall that connects the old museum's wings.

faq.q: Which famous houses should architecture students study?
faq.a: A core list: Frank Lloyd Wright's Robie House in Chicago (1910) and Fallingwater (completed 1937); the Rietveld Schröder House in Utrecht (1924); Le Corbusier's Villa Savoye in Poissy, built 1928 to 1931; Mies van der Rohe's Villa Tugendhat (1930) and Farnsworth House (1951); Alvar Aalto's Villa Mairea (1939); the Eames House (1949); and Robert Venturi's Vanna Venturi House (1964).

faq.q: Why are houses important in architecture?
faq.a: Houses matter because they are small buildings that make large arguments. A house can voice the views of those who build or inhabit it, and the materials close to hand shape its form, so one house can lay out an entire way of building. Villa Savoye, made of reinforced concrete, gathers Le Corbusier's Five Points of Architecture in a single house and had a huge influence on modernism.

faq.q: What were the Case Study Houses?
faq.a: The Case Study Houses were a programme, announced in January 1945 in Arts & Architecture, John Entenza's magazine, to produce low-cost, modern model homes able to be built many times over. The best known is the Eames House (1949) in Los Angeles, which Charles and Ray Eames built for themselves out of mass-produced parts.

faq.q: What are the most famous modernist glass houses?
faq.a: The best known include the Farnsworth House in Plano (1951) by Mies van der Rohe, one glass room raised on eight steel columns over a floodplain, a steel-and-glass box in the International Style. Philip Johnson's Glass House in New Canaan (1949) is a glass box with the landscape for walls; only the bathroom is closed off. Earlier, Mies's Villa Tugendhat in Brno (1930) has glass walls that drop away to the garden.

faq.q: What makes good library architecture?
faq.a: Good library architecture both stores books and draws people to them, and across history the weight has shifted from archive towards public room. Libraries now also serve as community hubs. Helsinki Central Library Oodi (2018) spans an open ground floor with a timber wave clad in spruce, beneath a top-floor reading room known as book heaven, and Dokk1 in Aarhus (2015) brings library and citizens' services together on the waterfront.

faq.q: Which libraries should architecture students study?
faq.a: Start with the Bibliothèque Sainte-Geneviève by Henri Labrouste, opened in 1851 in Paris and seen as a major step on the way to modern architecture for its exposed cast-iron columns and arches. Then compare Gunnar Asplund's Stockholm Public Library (1928), Alvar Aalto's Viipuri Library (1935), lit by round conical skylights, the Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library (1963), the Geisel Library in San Diego (1970) and Mecanoo's Library of Birmingham (2013).

faq.q: How has library design changed over time?
faq.a: Over time the emphasis has shifted from keeping records to welcoming the public. The earliest libraries, such as Mesopotamia's Library of Ashurbanipal, were archives of early writing. Growing collections later ran out of room, which brought in compact shelving that moves on tracks. The United States built 1,689 Carnegie libraries from 1883 to 1929, and modernism shaped the public libraries of the 1960s. Recent libraries add public rooms, from Oodi in Helsinki to Calgary Central Library (2018).

faq.q: What are good examples of modern libraries?
faq.a: Alberto Kalach's Vasconcelos Library in Mexico City (2006) hangs steel book stacks in a tall glazed hall within a botanical garden. Snøhetta's Bibliotheca Alexandrina (2002) lights a terraced reading room through a tilted disc roof, behind a granite wall of scripts. Mecanoo's Library of Birmingham (2013) stacks boxes wrapped in interlocking metal rings, with a rotunda reading room and garden terraces, and Oodi in Helsinki (2018) opens its ground floor to the city.

faq.q: What is a pavilion in architecture?
faq.a: A pavilion is a secondary building, either standing apart from a main building or joined to it, and traditionally it was made for pleasure and rest. The word comes from a big tent held up on posts. Today it also means the national pavilions at world's fairs and art biennales, which are mostly temporary and dismantled once the fair ends.

faq.q: Why are pavilions important in architecture?
faq.a: Pavilions matter because, being small and often temporary, they allow architects to try out an idea at full scale. In the Barcelona Pavilion (1929) by Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich, freestanding walls stand beneath a floating roof, and space flows rather than forming rooms. At Expo 2000 in Hanover, Shigeru Ban's Japan Pavilion was a gridshell made of recycled paper tubes, and Buckminster Fuller's Montreal Biosphère (1967) is a geodesic dome of steel tubes.

faq.q: What is the Serpentine Pavilion?
faq.a: The Serpentine Pavilion is a temporary summer pavilion that the Serpentine Galleries in London have commissioned each year since 2000, always from a leading architect. Like most fair pavilions, each one comes down when its season ends, so it serves as a full-scale test of an architect's ideas. Venice's Giardini offers a permanent counterpart, with 30 national pavilions, some designed by major 20th-century architects, for example Sverre Fehn's Nordic Pavilion (1962).

faq.q: Which world's fair pavilions should architecture students study?
faq.a: Compare the Barcelona Pavilion (1929); the Atomium in Brussels (1958), nine steel spheres in an iron-crystal pattern; the Montreal Biosphère (1967); Álvaro Siza's Portugal Pavilion in Lisbon (1998), whose thin concrete canopy hangs like a sheet between two porticoes; the Netherlands Pavilion by MVRDV (Expo 2000), a vertical park built from stacked Dutch landscapes; and the China Pavilion by He Jingtang (Expo 2010), based on dougong timber brackets.

faq.q: What is social housing in architecture?
faq.a: Social housing, also called public housing, means subsidised or affordable homes, usually in larger buildings. Municipal housing in its modern form grew out of rapid population growth in cities. Britain started building council houses on a mass scale around 1920, following the 1919 Addison Act, with tower blocks arriving in the 1950s. Red Vienna set large blocks such as the Karl-Marx-Hof (1930) around green courts.

faq.q: Which housing projects should architecture students study?
faq.a: In date order: the Hufeisensiedlung (1927) in Berlin by Bruno Taut and Martin Wagner, a horseshoe wrapped around a pond; the Weissenhof Estate in Stuttgart (1927); Vienna's Karl-Marx-Hof (1930); the Unité d'Habitation (1952) by Le Corbusier in Marseille; Park Hill in Sheffield (1961); Habitat 67 in Montréal (1967); the Barbican Estate in London (1982); and Quinta Monroy (2004) in Iquique, Chile, by Alejandro Aravena.

faq.q: What does "streets in the sky" mean?
faq.a: "Streets in the sky" means housing in which broad access corridors or decks act as streets raised above the ground. The Unité d'Habitation (1952) in Marseille, by Le Corbusier, holds 337 flats, with an internal street on every third floor and a communal terrace on its flat roof. Park Hill (1961) in Sheffield moves those streets outdoors as broad concrete decks following the slope, and London's Balfron Tower (1967) connects its flats to a separate service tower by bridges.

faq.q: What is incremental housing?
faq.a: Incremental housing builds part of a home properly and leaves residents to complete the rest when they can. At Quinta Monroy (2004) in Iquique, Chile, Alejandro Aravena built half of a good house for each family and left them the other half to finish; the approach helped him win the 2016 Pritzker Prize. It is a useful precedent for any student project on affordable housing.

faq.q: What is sacred architecture?
faq.a: Sacred architecture means designing and constructing places of worship, where a building's plan and form express belief. Temples in the ancient world were often thought of as the home of a god. A Hindu temple is understood as a model of inner space as well as of the universe, with a tower over its sanctum known as the shikhara, or the vimana in the south. Bahá'í houses of worship have nine sides and nine entrances.

faq.q: How did mosque architecture develop?
faq.a: Mosques began as hypostyle halls, first developed under the Umayyads, with courtyards to hold the Friday prayer crowds. In the 15th century the Ottomans brought in the central-dome mosque: in Istanbul, Mimar Sinan's Süleymaniye Mosque (1557) braces its dome with half-domes, and in Edirne the Selimiye Mosque (1575) rests a single wide dome on eight piers. Modern mosques reinterpret both types, as Marina Tabassum's Bait Ur Rouf Mosque in Dhaka (2012) does.

faq.q: Which religious buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: Start with Hagia Sophia (537) in Istanbul, among the earliest buildings to have a fully pendentive dome. Mali's Great Mosque of Djenné (1907) is made of mud brick, with palm-wood beams kept in place as permanent scaffolding. Then compare Notre-Dame du Haut (1955) in Ronchamp by Le Corbusier, Oscar Niemeyer's Cathedral of Brasília (1970), the Church of the Light (1989) by Tadao Ando and the Lotus Temple in New Delhi (1986).

faq.q: How did modern materials change church design?
faq.a: Steel and concrete changed the way churches were designed in the 20th century. In Tokyo, Kenzo Tange's St. Mary's Cathedral (1964) brings eight hyperbolic paraboloid shells together in a cross-shaped skylight; Niemeyer's Cathedral of Brasília surrounds a sunken nave with sixteen curved concrete columns; and Ando cuts a cross of light into a concrete wall. Gothic, by contrast, which began with Saint-Denis's abbey church in 12th-century France, was defined by the pointed arch.

faq.q: Why does school architecture matter?
faq.a: School architecture matters because a building's design can have a strong effect on how students learn, so plan, light and shared spaces become part of the teaching. During the late 1960s and the 1970s, open classrooms grew popular across North America. The Rolex Learning Center (2010) in Lausanne by SANAA carries the idea further, with one continuous floor that rises and falls in hills and valleys, cut through by patios, instead of stairs and walls.

faq.q: What is the difference between an American campus and a British university?
faq.a: One contrast comes from Patrick Abercrombie in 1922: American campuses spread their departments through a park, among the trees, while Oxford and Cambridge are built around formal quadrangles. Traditionally, a campus is a college or university's land and buildings. Gothic, which thrived in English universities between the 13th and 15th centuries, was later revived on campuses, for example at Pittsburgh's Cathedral of Learning (1937).

faq.q: Which school and campus buildings should architecture students study?
faq.a: Start with the Bauhaus, which Walter Gropius set up on 1 April 1919 in Weimar; his Bauhaus Dessau (1926) encloses the workshops behind a glass curtain wall, laid out on a pinwheel plan. Then compare Mackintosh's Glasgow School of Art (1909), Mies's S. R. Crown Hall in Chicago (1956), Le Corbusier's Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts (1963), Louis Kahn's Phillips Exeter Academy Library (1971) and Herzog & de Meuron's Blavatnik School of Government in Oxford (2015).

faq.q: Why are so many university buildings brutalist?
faq.a: Brutalism was a common choice for university campuses worldwide in the 1960s and 1970s. Paul Rudolph's Yale Art and Architecture Building (1963) is a design studio built in section, with dozens of interlocking levels. Vilanova Artigas's FAU-USP in São Paulo (1969) puts an architecture school under one great roof, joined by ramps, and Denys Lasdun's ziggurats at the University of East Anglia (1968) step down to a lake.

faq.q: What is memorial architecture?
faq.a: Memorial architecture gives memory a physical place: a memorial is any object or place on which memory or commemoration centres. Gravestones and plaques are the commonest kind, and temporary, improvised memorials are known as grassroots memorials. Mausoleums are monuments built around a burial chamber, and their name comes from Mausolus's tomb at Halicarnassus. Atatürk's mausoleum, Anitkabir in Ankara (1953), is one modern example.

faq.q: Which memorials should architecture students study?
faq.a: Compare the Taj Mahal (1653) in Agra, whose white marble tomb stands on a raised plinth within a quartered garden; the Gateway Arch in St. Louis (1965) by Eero Saarinen; Igualada Cemetery (1994) by Enric Miralles and Carme Pinós, a path cut into a former quarry; the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe (2005) in Berlin by Peter Eisenman; and the National September 11 Memorial in New York (2011) by Michael Arad and Peter Walker.

faq.q: Why was the Vietnam Veterans Memorial controversial?
faq.a: Its colour, its lack of ornament and its form sunk below ground were what made Maya Lin's Vietnam Veterans Memorial controversial at first. The memorial, dedicated in 1982, consists of two black granite walls. It is a useful case for students because each of those three choices, material, decoration and section, is what gives the memorial its meaning, and each was what critics first objected to.

faq.q: How does the Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe work?
faq.a: It works through 2,711 concrete stelae of different heights, arranged on a sloping grid so that visitors walk through the narrow aisles between them. Peter Eisenman's memorial in Berlin opened in 2005. The stelae carry no names or information, which critics have said weakens its message. Compare it with the National September 11 Memorial, where two square voids mark the towers' footprints.

faq.q: Why is London's architecture worth studying?
faq.a: London is worth studying because it has been rebuilt many times over on the same ground. The turning point was the Great Fire of 1666, which wiped out roughly nine tenths of the city. Wren's grid plan was dropped, and rebuilding followed the medieval street pattern, under an act of 1667 that called for brick houses of a uniform height and plot size. Later, Victorian London built an underground railway before any other city in the world.

faq.q: Which modern buildings in London should architecture students visit?
faq.a: A good route takes in Denys Lasdun's Royal National Theatre (1976), whose concrete terraces step toward the Thames; the Barbican Estate (1982); Richard Rogers's Lloyd's Building (1986); Tate Modern (2000), a power station turned museum; Foster and Partners' 30 St Mary Axe (2004), a diagrid tower; and Renzo Piano's The Shard (2012), London's first supertall skyscraper.

faq.q: Where can I see brutalist architecture in London?
faq.a: London has some of the best-known brutalist buildings anywhere. The Barbican Estate and Barbican Centre (1982) lift housing, an arts centre and a lake onto walkways above the street. Ernő Goldfinger's Balfron Tower (1967) and Trellick Tower (1972) put their lifts in separate towers linked to the flats by bridges every third floor, and the Royal National Theatre (1976) sits on the South Bank.

faq.q: Which historic buildings in London should architecture students know?
faq.a: St Paul's Cathedral comes first: Pevsner ranked Wren's dome there among the world's most perfect. John Nash planned Regent Street together with James Burton and turned Buckingham House into Buckingham Palace. Sir John Soane's Museum (1824) draws daylight down through narrow, layered rooms, and Charles Barry and Augustus Pugin's Palace of Westminster (1876) covers the parliament building with Perpendicular Gothic Revival detail.

faq.q: Why is New York's architecture worth studying?
faq.a: New York is worth studying because it holds one of the world's biggest and most varied sets of skyscrapers, shaped by its own rules. Under the 1916 Zoning Resolution, buildings had to step back and towers could occupy only a set share of the lot, which is where Art Deco towers such as the Empire State and Chrysler buildings got their tapering tops. Grand Central Terminal follows the Beaux-Arts style.

faq.q: Which skyscrapers in New York should architecture students study?
faq.a: In date order: the Flatiron Building (1902), which fills a triangular block; the Woolworth Building (1913) by Cass Gilbert, a steel frame clad in Gothic Revival terracotta; the Chrysler Building (1930), placed by many historians and architects among the city's best; the Empire State Building (1931), the first to rise beyond 100 storeys; the Seagram Building (1958); and 56 Leonard Street (2017) by Herzog & de Meuron.

faq.q: Which modern buildings in New York should architecture students visit?
faq.a: Good stops include Frank Lloyd Wright's Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum (1959), where a single spiral ramp takes the place of floors, and the Seagram Building (1958) by Mies van der Rohe, set back behind a plaza and described by the critic Paul Goldberger as among the city's most copied buildings. Add Eero Saarinen's TWA Flight Center (1962), the Ford Foundation Building (1967) with its glazed garden atrium, and the High Line (2009), a railway converted into a park.

faq.q: What are the best examples of International Style buildings in New York?
faq.a: Two of the earliest influential American examples of the International Style are in New York: 330 West 42nd Street and the Seagram Building. The wall also lets you compare the United Nations Headquarters (1952), a thin Secretariat slab with glass curtain-wall faces; SOM's Manufacturers Trust Company Building (1954), a glass-walled bank on Fifth Avenue; and the Seagram Building itself (1958), whose bronze mullions show its frame.

faq.q: Why is Chicago important in architecture?
faq.a: Chicago matters because it is the city where the skyscraper was developed. Once the 1871 Great Chicago Fire had wiped out most of downtown, the city was rebuilt. The Montauk Building (1882–83) was the first building to carry the name skyscraper, and the Home Insurance Building (1885) by Jenney is regarded as the earliest whose structural frame included steel. With a steel skeleton, a building's height no longer depended on how strong its walls were.

faq.q: What is the Chicago School of architecture?
faq.a: The Chicago School was the architecture that came out of the city's rebuilding on steel frames, which released height from dependence on wall strength. Louis Sullivan dropped historical precedent in favour of emphasising height. The Reliance Building (1895) was the first skyscraper whose surface was mostly large plate-glass windows. From 1963, the work Mies van der Rohe did at IIT, where his S. R. Crown Hall (1956) stands, gave rise to a "Second Chicago School".

faq.q: Which buildings in Chicago should architecture students visit?
faq.a: Start with Burnham & Root's Rookery Building (1888) and the Monadnock Building (1893); no load-bearing masonry building ever built has been taller. Add Frank Lloyd Wright's Robie House (1910); 860-880 Lake Shore Drive by Mies (1951), a pair of steel-and-glass towers set at right angles; the John Hancock Center (1969) and Willis Tower (1973) by Bruce Graham and Fazlur Khan; and Jeanne Gang's Aqua Tower (2009), whose balconies form undulating contours.

faq.q: Who were the most important Chicago architects?
faq.a: The key names start with Daniel Burnham, who led the design of the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition, the "White City", and with John Root built the Rookery and the Monadnock. Then Louis Sullivan, whose Sullivan Center sets a white terracotta grid over an ornate cast-iron base. Later came Mies van der Rohe, whose work at IIT started a Second Chicago School, and SOM's Bruce Graham and Fazlur Khan, who designed the John Hancock Center's X-braced tube.

faq.q: Why is Paris important in architecture?
faq.a: Paris matters because new styles began there. Gothic started with the rebuilt choir of Saint-Denis, completed in 1144; about 1160 Maurice de Sully applied it on a much bigger scale at Notre-Dame, and the upper chapel of Sainte-Chapelle is described as the finest example of the new style. Rebuilding of the Louvre's Lescot wing in the French Renaissance style started in 1546.

faq.q: How did Haussmann change Paris?
faq.a: Haussmann led a rebuilding of Paris that began in 1853, when Napoleon III appointed him the Seine's prefect, and ended with his dismissal in January 1870. That work rested on older rules: formal height limits on the city's buildings dated back to 1667. The Palais Garnier (1875) by Charles Garnier comes from the same period.

faq.q: Which modern buildings in Paris should architecture students visit?
faq.a: Begin with the Centre Pompidou (1977), the Piano and Rogers design picked from 681 entries to a competition, which places its colour-coded services and structure outside. Then compare the Louvre Pyramid (1989) by I. M. Pei, Bernard Tschumi's parc de la Villette (1987), a grid of red follies, Jean Nouvel's Fondation Cartier (1994) and Musée du quai Branly (2006), and Frank Gehry's Fondation Louis Vuitton (2014), with its twelve curved glass sails.

faq.q: What did the world's fairs leave in Paris?
faq.a: They left the Eiffel Tower, from the 1889 fair, and the Grand Palais, from the 1900 one. Gustave Eiffel's tower draws four curving wrought-iron legs together into one tapering shaft. The Grand Palais by Charles Girault conceals a vaulted nave of riveted steel and glass behind stone Beaux-Arts facades, and his Petit Palais, built the same year, arranges top-lit galleries around a semicircular garden court.

faq.q: Why is Berlin's architecture worth studying?
faq.a: Berlin is worth studying because its buildings record the city's 20th century, from the reforms of the Weimar years through the Cold War and beyond. In the east, Karl-Marx-Allee (1949–1960) was built as a socialist-classicist showpiece of housing for workers; in the west, the Hansaviertel became the Interbau project, rebuilt with Gropius, Aalto, Niemeyer and others. Potsdamer Platz lay desolate through the Cold War and was rebuilt during the 1990s.

faq.q: Which modern buildings in Berlin should architecture students visit?
faq.a: Start with Hans Scharoun's Berliner Philharmonie (1963), whose vineyard terraces of seats surround the orchestra, and Mies van der Rohe's Neue Nationalgalerie (1968), one column-free glass hall. Then see Norman Foster's Reichstag dome (1999), Daniel Libeskind's Jewish Museum Berlin (2001), a deconstructivist zigzag cut through by voids, Peter Eisenman's Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe (2005) and David Chipperfield's James Simon Gallery (2019).

faq.q: What are the Berlin Modernism Housing Estates?
faq.a: They are seven housing estates from the Weimar years, by Martin Wagner, Bruno Taut and others, which together form a World Heritage group and influenced housing well outside Germany. Taut's Gartenstadt Falkenberg (1916), known as the paintbox estate, gives its garden-city terraces bold colours, and the Hufeisensiedlung (1927) by Taut and Wagner curves its housing into a horseshoe around a pond.

faq.q: Who was Karl Friedrich Schinkel?
faq.a: Karl Friedrich Schinkel was the architect who shaped Berlin's classical core. He designed the Altes Museum on Museum Island, which opened in 1830 behind a colonnade of eighteen Ionic columns, and national art museums elsewhere later took it as their model. His Bauakademie (1836, demolished 1962) is seen as anticipating modern architecture. The other museums on Museum Island were built across a century, the first under the Prussian kings.

faq.q: Why is Tokyo important for modern architecture?
faq.a: Tokyo is a key city for studying modern Japanese architecture, even though its buildings follow no one style. Twice in recent history it was reduced to ruins and rebuilt: the 1923 Great Kanto earthquake opened an era of concrete construction, and a March 1945 air raid burned large parts of the city. The 1964 Olympics signalled its rebirth as a modern city.

faq.q: What is Metabolism in architecture?
faq.a: Metabolism is an architectural movement launched through a manifesto prepared for Tokyo's 1960 World Design Conference, which saw the city as a living organism that keeps renewing itself. Kenzo Tange acted as a mentor to the Metabolists but did not join them. The Nakagin Capsule Tower (1972) by Kisho Kurokawa attaches prefabricated capsules to two cores, applying the Metabolist idea of replaceable parts, and it pioneered capsule architecture.

faq.q: Which buildings in Tokyo should architecture students visit?
faq.a: Begin with Le Corbusier's National Museum of Western Art (1959) and Kenzo Tange's Yoyogi National Gymnasium (1964), whose suspension roof hangs from two concrete masts and which his Pritzker citation praised. Add Tange's St. Mary's Cathedral (1964), Fumihiko Maki's Spiral (1985), Rafael Viñoly's Tokyo International Forum (1996), Renzo Piano's Maison Hermès (2001) and Kengo Kuma's Japan National Stadium (2019).

faq.q: How do Tokyo's buildings deal with earthquakes?
faq.a: After the 1923 Great Kanto earthquake the city moved toward concrete construction. On the wall, Renzo Piano's Maison Hermès (2001) sets its glass-block skin on a frame designed to flex in earthquakes, and Nikken Sekkei's Tokyo Skytree (2012) uses a concrete core as a damping column, like the central column of a pagoda, as its triangular base turns into a round plan.

faq.q: Why is Barcelona important in architecture?
faq.a: Barcelona matters chiefly for a single plan and a single movement. Ildefons Cerdà's 1859 Eixample, the largest expansion the city has seen, set out a grid of broad avenues and blocks with cut-off corners. Modernisme lasted from Barcelona's first World Fair, held in 1888, until 1911. Earlier layers remain as well: the city started as the Roman town of Barcino, and its oldest parts are in the Gothic Quarter.

faq.q: Which Gaudí buildings should architecture students visit?
faq.a: Start with Casa Vicens (1885), Antoni Gaudí's first major project; Palau Güell (1890), whose central hall sits beneath a perforated dome; Casa Batlló (1906), where tiles in the light well shade from deep to pale blue so the daylight is even throughout; Casa Milà (1912) and its undulating stone facade; Park Güell (1914); and the Sagrada Familia, started in 1882. Gaudí is the most famous Modernisme architect.

faq.q: Who was Domènech i Montaner?
faq.a: Lluís Domènech i Montaner was a Modernisme architect whose work gave a real alternative to Gaudí's. His Palau de la Música Catalana (1908) relies on a steel frame to open up glass walls and a stained-glass skylight above the concert hall. His Hospital de Sant Pau places brick ward pavilions among gardens, joined by underground service tunnels, so the hospital reads as a garden of small buildings.

faq.q: Which modern buildings in Barcelona should architecture students visit?
faq.a: Start with the Barcelona Pavilion by Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich: built for the 1929 Exposition, it was pulled down in 1930 and permanently reconstructed in 1983–86. Then see Josep Lluís Sert's Fundació Joan Miró (1975), Arata Isozaki's Palau Sant Jordi (1990), Jean Nouvel's Torre Glòries (2005), Enric Ruiz-Geli's Media-TIC (2010), wrapped in ETFE cushions, and Lacol's La Borda (2018), cooperative housing in cross-laminated timber.

faq.q: What is Los Angeles architecture known for?
faq.a: Los Angeles is known above all for its modern houses, though its styles range widely, from Mission Revival onward. The Case Study Houses changed the way American homes were designed. Googie, a Space Age roadside style, took its name from a Hollywood coffee shop. The Los Angeles Conservancy was set up in 1978 to rescue the Central Library from demolition.

faq.q: Which Case Study Houses should architecture students know?
faq.a: Two to know are the Eames House (1949), which Charles and Ray Eames built with industrial parts bought off the shelf, and the Stahl House by Pierre Koenig (1960), also called Case Study House #22, an L-shaped steel-and-glass pavilion cantilevered over the Hollywood Hills whose photograph is among Los Angeles's most famous. Arts & Architecture started the programme in 1945, asking for houses that could be repeated rather than one-off performances.

faq.q: Which modern houses in Los Angeles should architecture students visit?
faq.a: Begin with Frank Lloyd Wright's Hollyhock House (1921), which he called his "California Romanza", and Rudolph Schindler's house (1922), a live/work experiment for two families that set a precedent for California architecture. Then see Richard Neutra's Lovell Health House (1929), often called the first steel-frame house in the US, the Eames House (1949), John Lautner's Chemosphere (1960) and the Stahl House (1960).

faq.q: Which public buildings in Los Angeles should architecture students study?
faq.a: Start with the Walt Disney Concert Hall (2003) by Frank Gehry, where curved stainless steel, chosen in place of the stone first planned, encloses a vineyard-style hall. Compare Richard Meier's Getty Center (1997), a hilltop campus on two shifted grids; Rafael Moneo's Cathedral of Our Lady of the Angels (2002), lit through alabaster windows; and Morphosis's Caltrans District 7 Headquarters (2004), an office slab in a perforated aluminium skin.

faq.q: What is adaptive reuse in architecture?
faq.a: Adaptive reuse means putting an existing building to a new use rather than demolishing it. This saves the expense of demolition, retains the energy already invested in the original structure and preserves a community's connection to its past. Old buildings can also supply materials to new projects. Tate Modern in London, a gallery in a power station that opened in 2000, is a classic example.

faq.q: What are good examples of adaptive reuse?
faq.a: Good examples include Paris's Musée d'Orsay (1986), set inside a former railway station, and the SESC Pompéia (1986) in São Paulo by Lina Bo Bardi, which retains a drum factory and uses it as a leisure centre. Tate Modern's Turbine Hall has become an indoor street; New York's High Line (2009) is a park laid along an old elevated railway; and Hamburg's Elbphilharmonie (2017) puts a glass crown on top of a brick warehouse.

faq.q: What are the challenges of adaptive reuse?
faq.a: The main challenges are the existing structure and building codes, which is why a condition survey determines whether a project is viable. Designers then must choose what to keep and where a new opening can be cut into the old structure. At Zeitz MOCAA (2017) in Cape Town, a grain silo is carved into an atrium in the shape of a single corn kernel, and Peter Zumthor's Kolumba Museum (2007) builds a brick veil over a ruined Gothic church.

faq.q: How do architects add new parts to old buildings?
faq.a: Compare three approaches. Carlo Scarpa's Castelvecchio Museum in Verona (1975) reworks a medieval castle with precise new joints, cuts and display stands. OMA's Fondazione Prada in Milan (2015) joins former distillery buildings with new galleries and a tower. Zaha Hadid Architects' Port House in Antwerp (2016) hovers a faceted glass extension, shaped like a ship's bow, on concrete piers above an old fire station.

faq.q: What is a cantilever in architecture?
faq.a: A cantilever is a structural part anchored at one end and unsupported at the other, which lets a building project outward with nothing holding it up from below. In traditional timber-framed buildings, an upper floor that juts out this way is called a jetty. Bridges can be built out from each side as matching pairs of cantilevers that join at the centre. At Fallingwater, Frank Lloyd Wright used cantilevers to carry large balconies out over a waterfall.

faq.q: What are famous examples of cantilevers in architecture?
faq.a: Famous examples include Wright's Robie House (1910) in Chicago, whose long roofs reach out from the core rather than sitting on walls, and Fallingwater, where concrete terraces supported at one end only extend out from the chimney. In Asmara, the Fiat Tagliero Building (1938) by Giuseppe Pettazzi projects two 15 m concrete wings from a central tower, and in Beijing OMA's CCTV Headquarters (2012) links two leaning towers with a 75-metre cantilever.

faq.q: Which building has the longest cantilever roof?
faq.a: The Busan Cinema Center (2011) in South Korea, by Coop Himmelb(l)au, is described in its caption as having the longest cantilever roof in the world, resting on a single cone above an outdoor theatre. Other long reaches on the wall include Moshe Safdie's Marina Bay Sands in Singapore (2010), whose sky park cantilevers far beyond the north tower, and Jean Nouvel's Guthrie Theater in Minneapolis (2006), with a long bridge reaching toward the Mississippi.

faq.q: How do cantilevers shape towers?
faq.a: In a tower the cantilever can come from the core rather than the walls. Wright's Price Tower (1956), his only built skyscraper, cantilevers its floors like branches from a central core. BBPR's Torre Velasca in Milan (1958) pushes its upper residential floors out on angled ribs, and Herzog & de Meuron's 56 Leonard Street in New York (2017) shifts and cantilevers its floor plates so each flat gets its own outline.

faq.q: What is a courtyard in architecture?
faq.a: A courtyard is a space open to the sky, often enclosed by a building, that brings light, air and privacy into the heart of a plan, qualities wanted almost everywhere. When the weather is warm, an open central court helps keep a house cool. Courtyard houses date from the Neolithic, roughly 6400–6000 BC, and in a Roman house the open central space was known as the atrium.

faq.q: What are good examples of courtyard architecture?
faq.a: Good examples start with the Alhambra in Granada, where the palace is built up from rectangular courtyards as its basic unit. In Isfahan, the Shah Mosque (1629) sets four monumental iwans around its central courtyard. Louis Kahn's Salk Institute (1965) arranges its labs around a travertine plaza that opens to the Pacific, and Alvar Aalto's Säynätsalo Town Hall (1952) groups brick rooms around a raised courtyard of grass.

faq.q: Which courtyard houses should architecture students study?
faq.a: For modern courtyard houses, compare Luis Barragán's house in Mexico City (1948), Alvar Aalto's Villa Mairea (1939), with its L-shaped courtyard, and the Row House in Sumiyoshi (1976) by Tadao Ando, whose interior courtyard admits light and must be crossed to move between rooms. The type is old: the ancient Middle East used courtyards widely, and in the old towns of Morocco, houses have always been built around courtyards as the norm.

faq.q: How do contemporary buildings use courtyards?
faq.a: Contemporary buildings still use the courtyard to organise large plans. In I. M. Pei's Suzhou Museum (2006), white walls enclose a water garden. The Interlace in Singapore (2013), by OMA and Ole Scheeren, stacks thirty-one blocks in a hexagonal weave that creates large garden courtyards. In Washington, D.C., the Kogod Courtyard (2007) at the National Portrait Gallery, by Foster + Partners, roofs a 19th-century courtyard with a rippling glass canopy.

faq.q: What is a brise-soleil?
faq.a: A brise-soleil is a sunshade screen on a facade; the French name means "sun breaker", and it lowers a building's heat gain by turning sunlight away. Its plainest form is a horizontal overhang on the side facing the sun. It is used mostly on glass facades at risk of overheating, yet it still lets low morning, evening and winter sun through, which means louvres can also warm a building passively.

faq.q: How did Le Corbusier use the brise-soleil?
faq.a: Le Corbusier made patterned concrete versions popular. In Chandigarh, his Palace of Assembly (1962) is a parliament designed for the Punjab sun; the Secretariat Building (1958) runs a grid of brise-soleil along a long concrete slab; and the Palace of Justice (1955) shelters its courts beneath a huge concrete parasol roof. In Ahmedabad, the Mill Owners' Association Building (1954) uses angled concrete fins.

faq.q: What are good examples of brise-soleil in architecture?
faq.a: In Rio de Janeiro, the Gustavo Capanema Palace (1945) by Lúcio Costa and Oscar Niemeyer fits adjustable brise-soleil to an office slab, and in São Paulo Niemeyer's Copan Building (1966) runs continuous horizontal sunshades along a serpentine slab. The New York Times Building (2007) by Renzo Piano screens its glass walls with ceramic rods, and in Seoul David Chipperfield's Amorepacific Headquarters (2017) wraps a near-cube in vertical sun screens.

faq.q: Can a brise-soleil move?
faq.a: Yes. Santiago Calatrava designed a moving one: above a glass hall at the Milwaukee Art Museum's Quadracci Pavilion (2001), a wing-shaped sunscreen of steel fins opens and folds. In Paris, the Institut du Monde Arabe uses 240 photo-sensitive, motor-driven apertures as a brise-soleil, which open and close to control the light that reaches the interior.

faq.q: What is mass timber?
faq.a: Mass timber means large engineered wood components that form a building's structure. One type, cross-laminated timber (CLT), lays boards in layers set at right angles to each other for strength and is used in roofs, floors and walls. Buildings in mass timber are quicker to put up than those in steel or concrete and behave very well in earthquakes. In Barcelona, Lacol's La Borda (2018) is cooperative housing made of cross-laminated timber.

faq.q: What are good examples of timber architecture?
faq.a: Compare Alvar Aalto's Villa Mairea (1939), modernism softened with timber; E. Fay Jones's Thorncrown Chapel (1980), a lattice of small pine members sized to be carried by hand; Renzo Piano's Jean-Marie Tjibaou Cultural Centre (1998); Shigeru Ban's Centre Pompidou-Metz (2010), under a woven glulam grid; K2S's Kamppi Chapel in Helsinki (2012); and Kengo Kuma's Japan National Stadium (2019), with timber louvres from all 47 prefectures.

faq.q: What is the tallest wooden building?
faq.a: When it was completed in 2019, Mjøstårnet in Brumunddal, Norway, by Voll Arkitekter, was the tallest wooden building in the world: a glulam frame of 18 storeys. As for the largest, the Metropol Parasol (2011) in Seville by J. Mayer H. is marketed as the biggest wooden structure in the world; its giant timber parasols shelter a market and Roman ruins, with a walkway on top.

faq.q: What are the oldest timber buildings?
faq.a: Building in wood is very old: Roman Herculaneum has the oldest known half-timbered building. The Pagoda of Fogong Temple in Yingxian (1056) is the oldest all-wood pagoda that survives in China, and Japan's Ise Grand Shrine is by tradition rebuilt in cypress wood once every 20 years, keeping the craft alive. Kyoto's Katsura Imperial Villa (17th century) shows tatami-module rooms and sliding screens.

faq.q: What is a tensile structure?
faq.a: A tensile structure works purely in tension, without compression or bending, and is a different thing from tensegrity. Since they can span great distances at low cost, tensile structures are mostly used as roofs, and pretensioning keeps their flexible elements rigid under load. In Tokyo, Kenzo Tange's Yoyogi National Gymnasium (1964) uses two concrete masts to hang its roof, and the Munich Olympic Stadium (1972) stretches a cable-net roof over its seating.

faq.q: Who was Frei Otto?
faq.a: Frei Otto was a champion of tensile structures. In 1964 he set up Stuttgart's Institute for Lightweight Structures. He first used a tensile roof for West Germany's pavilion at Expo 67, then for the Munich Olympic Stadium (1972), designed with Behnisch & Partner, where acrylic glass panels sit in a cable-net roof. Before him, Vladimir Shukhov had been among the first to calculate the stresses in such structures.

faq.q: What are good examples of tensile structures?
faq.a: Start with the J. S. Dorton Arena (1952) in Raleigh by Maciej Nowicki, the world's first structure to have a roof supported by cables. Then compare Eero Saarinen's Washington Dulles Airport Terminal (1962), whose concrete roof hangs in a catenary curve; the Yoyogi National Gymnasium (1964); SOM's Hajj Terminal in Jeddah (1981); Eduardo Souto de Moura's Braga Municipal Stadium (2003); and Hopkins Architects' London Velodrome (2011), a cable-net roof shaped like the track.

faq.q: What materials are used for tensile roofs?
faq.a: Tensile roofs most commonly use fabrics of PTFE-coated fibreglass or PVC-coated polyester, while some use ETFE film, either as single layers or as cushions. In London, Richard Rogers's Millennium Dome (1999) suspends a PTFE-coated fabric roof by cables from twelve yellow masts. Shigeru Ban's Centre Pompidou-Metz (2010) stretches a PTFE membrane over a woven timber grid, and in Astana the Khan Shatyr Entertainment Center (2010) by Foster + Partners is a tilted tent of cable net and ETFE cushions.
